Don Huynh, Autumn Luinenburg, Jocelyn Matias, Bailey Ponto, 
Amarilyz Vega Hernandez, Hermela Yisak and Heidi Tarus 
 
Minnesota West Bluejays A Team # 17983 
Minnesota West Community & Technical College | Worthington, MN 
Plant the Moon Challenge | Spring 2024 | Professional/Undergraduate Division 
Grant Funded by NASA’s Minnesota Space Grant Consortium

Introduction & Theory 
As NASA is gearing up the Artemis Program to return people to the Moon, the idea of colonizing 
the moon and other celestial bodies comes to mind. Having colonies on the Moon or Mars 
would help with our exploration and understanding of space by setting up bases for scientists 
to live and work. When thinking about people living in colonies a big factor in human survival is 
meeting the basic needs of humans. These needs include access to shelter, clean water, and 
nutritious food. This Plant the Moon Challenge project aims to answer the question of how to 
best feed people in a moon colony without having to bring the food on the spacecraft by 
growing the food with minimal materials using Moon regolith. Specifically, this project looks to 
answer the question of which nutrient additives added to the lunar regolith promotes the 
growth of nutritious collard greens (B. oleracea). 
 
Prior research done by the Fall 2022 Minnesota West Bluejays research team, demonstrated 
that addition of a nitrogen source in the form of urea (48% nitrogen) increase plant growth of 
Collard Greens (B. oleracea) over no nitrogen added in a soil mixture of 50% lunar regolith, 25% 
top soil, and 25% peat moss. However, during initial research this team discovered that 
nitrogen is not the only essential nutrient plants need from the soil. Nitrogen, phosphorus, and 
calcium are all essential macronutrient for plants. Nitrogen is used in the synthesis of proteins, 
nucleic acids, and some vitamins needed for growth, phosphorus is used for the synthesis of 
nucleic acids and phospholipids, and calcium is used to regulate nutrient transport, build cell 
walls, and support enzyme function (Clark et al., 2018). The team decided to plant Collard 
Greens (Brassica oleracea) due to their high nutrient and low calorie content with one cup of 
chopped raw collard greens (36g) contains 11 calories, 1g of protein, 1.44g of fiber, 2g of 
carbohydrate, and less than 1g of fat and sugar (U.S. Department of Agriculture, 2019). Collard 
greens are also an excellent source of Vitamin A, Vitamin C, Vitamin K, calcium, potassium, 
folate, and antioxidant (Baby, n.d). 
 
The team understands that the nutrients in the leaves of the Collard green need to come from 
the nutrients in the soil. The necessary nitrogen can easily be added by including urea in the

soil; phosphorus and calcium can be added to the soil in the form of bone meal (Puisis, 2022). 
This team decided to investigate how the addition of urea (48% nitrogen), bone meal (2% 
nitrogen, 17% phosphorus, and 12% calcium), and the combination of urea and bone meal may 
affect plant growth. The independent variable is the type and mixture of nutrient additives 
(urea and/or bone meal) added to the soil. The dependent variables for this study included 
germination rate, soil pH, height of the plant, number of true leaves, and final leaf surface area. 
The team also planned to measure photosynthetic rate, but this was not performed due to the 
advisor being gone the last week of the grow period. These measurements were chosen to 
measure plant germination rate and to measure the amount of food Collard Greens (Brassica 
oleracea) could produce. 
 
We hypothesize that the germination rate between the four treatment groups will not differ; 
however, the Collard Greens (B. oleracea) grown in the pots containing both urea and bone 
meal will produce the tallest plants, have the most leaves, and will have the highest final leaf 
surface area. 
Experiment & Measurement Methods 
Initial Set-Up 
The initial set up was done following the initial experimental design shown in the diagram 
below:

One week before the grow period started, the soil was mixed at a ratio of 25% top soil, 25% 
peat moss, and 50% lunar regolith by volume and placed in the 20 pots. Top soil was included 
to add in some organic materials and the peat moss was added to increase water retention. The 
Minnesota West Bluejay Fall 2023 teams struggled with plant mortality due to lack of water 
retention caused by not including peat moss in the soil mixture. The team used colored popsicle 
stick placed in the back of the pot to identify the treatment groups. Blue is for the control, 
purple for the urea group, green for the bone meal group, and yellow for the urea & bone meal 
group. After the soil was mixed, each pot had the additives added as indicated on the diagram 
and were watered with 100ml of tap water. The treatments were established using the 
suggested fertilizing loading rate of 0.5 lb Nitrogen per 1000 ft2 (Swift & Hammond, 2020), that 
was used in prior research done at Minnesota West, and the suggested application of 10lbs per 
100sq ft of bone meal from the Earth Science Natural Bone Meal package. There were four 
treatments: no nutrient additions, 0.036 g of Urea per pot, 3.31g of bone meal per pot, and a 
combination of 0.036g of Urea and 3.31g of bone meal. 
 
During week 1 of the grow period, the students on the A Team picked one pot from each 
treatment and wrote an identifier name on the popsicle stick which was placed in the back of 
the pot next to the other popsicle stick indicating the treatment group. Four sets of pots were 
planted and measured by one student labeled “HY”, “AV”, “DH”, and “JM” with the exception 
of the pots labeled “A&B” which had two students working together. After labeling with an 
identifier, each pot was planted with three Collard Greens seeds and watered with 100ml of tap 
water. Over the course of the grow period, the set-up was kept indoors with a temperature of 
22°C with the set of pots placed under a grow light containing two 18” GE plant and aquarium 
bulbs on a 12-hour light: 12-hour dark timer. The grow light was placed 20 cm from the top of 
the table and stayed at that height for the duration of the experiment. 
 
Plant Care 
On Monday and Thursday of each week of the grow period, each pot was watered with 50ml of 
tap water. Based on the seed packet, B. oleracea should be thinned to be at least 30.48 cm (12

inches) apart; therefore, as the pots are 8.5cm in width, the plants were thinned to one 
seedling on Thursday, February 22nd after data collection by keeping the tallest plant in the pot. 
This gave the tallest seedling in each pot the best chance to grow as thinning is a common 
gardening practice. The plants were kept in the same spot and in the same room through the 
duration of the experiment and were moved away from the light source for a maximum of two 
hours on Thursday each week between 1pm and 3pm to take measurements and then replaced 
back in the same location after measuring. The experiment was cut short by one week due to 
the advisor being out of town during the last week of the grow period. 
 
Measurements 
The dependent variables for this experiment were the soil pH, primordial leaf emergence for 
germination rate, plant height, number of true leaves, and final leaf surface area. An additional 
planned dependent variable was photosynthetic rate; however, this was not collected during 
the last week due to the advisor being out of town. Primordial leaf emergence was used to 
collect data on germination rate of the plants. Germination rate was collected twice by visually 
observing of the number of germinated seeds 7 days (week 2) and 14 days (week 3) after 
planting. The soil pH, plant height measurement, and number of true leaves was collected by 
team members once a week on Thursday using the soil pH meter sent with the lunar regolith 
and a 15-cm ruler for seven weeks. Leaf surface area was collected during week seven on 
Tuesday, March 19th 2024 using the LeafByte App, https://zoegp.science/leafbyte. This was 
done by holding up a scale (a white piece of paper with four black dots in the shape of a square) 
behind the leaf, taking a picture with a smart phone, identifying the scale, and having the app 
calculate the square centimeters of the leaf. In addition, a top-view and side-view picture of the 
entire set-up was taken once a week on Thursday (Appendix B: Photos). Records of the data 
collected was kept on paper next to the set up and was entered each week into a Microsoft 
Excel spreadsheet data analysis. 
Analysis & Results 
Data was organized and stored in a Microsoft Excel file where the graphs were also generated. 
The calculation of averages and standard errors was done in Microsoft Excel. All other statistics

were done using Statistics Kingdom (https://www.statskingdom.com/). The results section 
including the formatting of the graphs was completed using a provided template by the advisor. 
Soil pH 
The pH of the soil was not influence by the application of urea, bone meal, or urea & bone 
meal. The soil pH was consistent over the seven weeks with an average measurement between 
7.6 and 7.9. When analyzing the data for the soil pH, the Shapiro-Wilk test did not show a 
significant departure from normality for the control group, W(5) = 0.89 , p = 0.465, the urea 
group, W(5) = 0.77 , p =0.068, the bone meal group, W(5) = 0.77 , p = 0.068, or the urea & bone 
meal group, W(5) = 0.77 , p = 0.068. Because the groups showed normality, a one-way ANOVA 
was performed to evaluate the relationship between the treatment groups and final soil pH. 
The ANOVA was not significant at the 0.05 level, F(3, 16) = 1.0769, p =0.3869.

Kruskal-Wallis H test indicated that there was a non-significant difference in the germination

For week two germination rate, the Shapiro-Wilk test showed a significance departure from the 
normality for the control group, W(5) = .55, p = .003, and the urea group, W(5) = .55, p = .003; 
however, there was not a significant departure from normality for the bone meal group, W(5) = 
.77, p = .069, or the urea & bone meal group, W(5) = .83, p = .179. Because the data did not 
show normality for all four groups, a Kruskal-Wallis H test was used to analyze the between 
group data. The Kruskal-Wallis H test indicated that there was a non-significant difference in 
the germination rate between the four groups, χ2(3) = 5.01, p = .171, with a mean rank score of 
12.7 for the control group, 12.7 for the urea group, 10.2 for the bone meal group, 6.4 for the 
urea & bone meal group.

Plant Height Growth 
When analyzing the data for the final plant height, the Shapiro-Wilk test did not show a 
significant departure from normality for the control group, W(5) = 0.78 , p = 0.077, the urea 
group, W(5) = 0.88 , p =0.360, the bone meal group, W(5) = 0.89 , p = 0.430, or the urea & bone 
meal group, W(4) = 0.94 , p = 0.866. Because the groups showed normality, a one-way ANOVA 
was performed to evaluate the relationship between the treatment groups and final plant 
height. The ANOVA was not significant at the 0.05 level, F(3, 15) = 1.6281, p =0.2249.

Number of True Leaves 
When analyzing the data for the final plant height, the Shapiro-Wilk test did not show a 
significant departure from normality for the control group, W(5) = 0.88 , p = 0.400, or the bone 
meal group, W(5) = 0.96 , p = 0.959; however, there was a significant departure from normality 
for the urea group, W(5) = 0.68 , p =0.019 and the urea & bone meal group, W(4) = 0.63 , p = 
0.017. Because the data did not show normality for all four groups, a Kruskal-Wallis H test was 
used to analyze the between group data. The Kruskal-Wallis H test indicated that there was a 
significant difference in the final number of true leaves between the four groups, χ2(3) = 8.95, p 
= .030, with a mean rank score of 3.9 for the control group, 11.9 for the urea group, 11.9 for the 
bone meal group, 12.88 for the urea & bone meal group. Although the Kruskal-Wallis H test 
identified that the mean ranks are not statistically equal the Mann-Whitney U test for multiple 
comparisons does not show enough evidence for a statistical difference between any pair of 
groups.

Discussion & Conclusion 
According to Wamelink et al. 2014, the pH of Moon regolith simulate is around 9.6. Although 
the team did not have a specific hypothesis about soil pH for the experiment, the data shows 
that the additives including the top soil and peat moss did lower the pH of the regolith; 
however, the soil pH did not change over the grow period. The pH of the soil was on the 
alkaline side (7.6-7.9) which is not ideal conditions for collard greens to grow. Collard greens 
prefer soil with a soil pH of 6.5 to 6.8 to prevent clubroot disease (Bonnie Plants, 2011). The 
team discovered that urea can be used to reduce the pH of the soil; however, bone meal is 
typically used to raise a soil’s pH over time and thus may not be a good additive for growing 
Collard Greens. Research shows that soil on the alkaline side can restrict the water supply to 
the roots (Buresh & Quilty, n.d) and can also cause iron, manganese, and phosphorus to 
become unavailable do to the soil chemistry (Albert, 2024). Future research looking at additives 
that reduce the pH of the soil to promote good growth is necessary if this is a food item grown 
to feed people living on the moon. The team suggests investigating the addition of typical 
additive such as elemental sulfur, aluminum sulfate, or sulfuric acid to lower the soil pH to the 
acceptable range to grow Collard greens before conducting further experiments on the addition 
of fertilizers containing nitrogen, phosphorous, and calcium. Alternatively, organic matter such 
as mulch, pine needles, peat moss, compost, and coffee grounds could be added to lower the 
pH level (MasterClass, 2021). A great sustainable choice might be coffee grounds if the

individuals living on the moon consume coffee. In addition, it would be interesting to look at if 
the plants in this experiment developed clubroot disease from the high pH by removing the 
plants from the soil and looking at the roots. 
 
The team was disappointed to not collect the photosynthesis rate for this experiment and 
suggest future teams to collect this data as it can be used to show how efficient and how well 
the plants are growing and generating potential food for humans. 
 
We hypothesized that the germination rate between the four treatment groups would not 
differ; however, the Collard Greens (B. oleracea) grown in the pots containing both urea and 
bone meal would produce the tallest plants, have the most leaves, and have the highest final 
leaf surface area. The experiment supported the first part of the hypothesis where the 
germination rate was not statistically different between the treatment groups – on average 2 to 
3 of the three seeds germinated. Only one pot in the urea & bone meal group did not have any 
seeds germinate. This is an encouraging result because it shows that seed germination is not 
influence by either the urea, the bone meal, or the urea & bone meal combination when added 
to the soil. This supports prior research done at Minnesota West that showed very high 
germination rates similar to what was seen in this experiment. 
 
The data does not support the second part of the hypothesis. In terms of the plant height and 
final leaf surface area the statistics showed that there was not a significant difference between 
the treatments. The final number of true leaves did show a significant difference; however, the 
multiple comparisons test did not show enough evidence for a statistical difference between 
any pair of groups. The team concludes that the lack of statistical significance is due to the small 
sample size of the treatment groups which reduced the testing power of the chosen statistical 
tests. We suggest doing this experiment again with a higher sample size in each treatment 
groups to see if the trends seen in this experiment are significant.

The treatments that contained urea show a trend towards having taller plants and the 
treatments that had either urea and/or bone meal show a trend towards having more true 
leave and thus a higher total leaf surface area compared to the control group. The addition of 
bone meal did not seem to add any further benefit to the urea. Furthermore, only 0.036g of 
urea is needed compared to 4.3 g bone meal for the pots used based on the suggested 
fertilizing load. Therefore, the team suggests just adding urea to the soil when growing collard 
greens in lunar regolith to increase the amount of leaf surface area and thus food for humans 
living on the Moon. This would reduce the payload on the spacecraft if the urea is brought to 
the Moon with the additional benefit of being able to potentially extract urea from the urine of 
the individuals living on the Moon to be used as a fertilizer.
